hints: Focus on what holds a pure Group 1 metal together, and remember it is not ions of opposite charge or shared pairs.
Both sodium and potassium form $+1$ cations with one delocalised electron each, but $\text{Na}^+$ is smaller than $\text{K}^+$ as it has fewer shells.
Connect smaller ionic radius to stronger electrostatic pull on the sea of electrons, and pick the statement that uses that exact metallic bonding language.
walkthrough:
**Identify the bonding in both metals**

Both sodium and potassium are metals, so they have giant metallic lattices. Think of positive cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.

Model: $\text{M}^+ \text{ surrounded by } e^- (\text{delocalised})$

**Compare the cations**

Both give $\text{M}^+$ ions with the same charge and same number of delocalised electrons per ion. The big difference is size.

Size: $\text{Na}^+ \text{ (2,8) is smaller than } \text{K}^+ \text{ (2,8,8)}$

**Link size to strength and melting point**

A smaller cation has higher charge density, so it pulls the delocalised electrons closer and more strongly. Stronger metallic bonding needs more energy to break, so melting point is higher for sodium.

options.A: This is the correct metallic bonding description. Stronger attraction between $\text{Na}^+$ cations and delocalised electrons due to smaller ionic radius explains the higher melting point of sodium compared to potassium.
options.B: This describes ionic bonding. There are no anions in a pure sample of sodium or potassium, only cations and delocalised electrons, so this cannot explain the difference.
options.C: This is too vague and uses the wrong language. Melting a metal does not just overcome attraction between neutral atoms, it overcomes attraction between cations and delocalised electrons. It also sounds like simple covalent or van der Waals forces.
options.D: This describes covalent bonding. Nuclei attracted to a shared pair of electrons is the covalent model, which does not apply to giant metallic structures like sodium and potassium.
